mainTopic: The future judgment of the nations: רומי, פרס and the others claim credit for helping ישראל learn תורה, and their excuses are rejected
overview: The גמרא continues its story of the future judgment, when the nations come to claim reward for תורה. Each nation enters separately with its scholars, so that each can hear what God says to it. רומי enters first because it is the most important kingdom, and the גמרא proves both its importance and the rule that the important one goes first. רומי claims it built markets, bathhouses and wealth for ישראל's sake. God shows it was all for itself, and since רומי has no תורה, it leaves disappointed. פרס follows with the same kind of claim about bridges, cities and wars, and is turned away the same way, and so is every other nation. The nations then argue that they never got the תורה, then that they never accepted it, then that God never forced them with a mountain as He did with ישראל. God answers that they did not even keep the seven מצוות they accepted. The amud ends as the גמרא asks whether the nations gained by being released from those מצוות, and מר בריה דרבינא begins an answer that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Each nation enters with its scholars, proven from a verse
steps.stepSummary: The story continues: each nation enters together with its scholars. The גמרא supports this from the פסוק 'ויאספו לאומים' and shows that the word לאום means a kingdom.
steps.simpleTranslation: Each nation comes in with its scholars, as it says: 'And let the peoples be assembled.' The word 'לאום' always means a kingdom, as it says: 'And one kingdom shall be stronger than the other kingdom.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the line from the story, that each nation enters on its own with its scholars, and brings a פסוק to back it up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks of 'לאומים' being gathered, in the plural. To read this as separate kingdoms, the גמרא proves from the פסוק about יעקב and עשו that לאום means a kingdom. So the nations are gathered kingdom by kingdom.

keyTerms.meaning: Scribes, the scholars of a nation
A nation; here shown to mean a kingdom
As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.english: with its scholars,
as it is said: 'And let the peoples be assembled,'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 43:9

phrases.english: and 'le'om' means nothing other than kingdom,
as it is said: 'And one kingdom shall be stronger than the other kingdom.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 25:23

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from the previous section of the daf.
steps.raayaObject: That the nations enter separately, kingdom by kingdom, with their scholars.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיהו 43:9, read with the help of בראשית 25:23, which shows that לאום means kingdom.

steps.title: Can anything be jumbled before God?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the nations need to be separated at all. Can there be any confusion before the הקדוש ברוך הוא?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there such a thing as a jumble before the Holy One, Blessed be He?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that the nations must stand apart so things don't get mixed up, since the הקדוש ברוך הוא sees everything clearly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Separating the nations sounds like it is for God's sake, so He can tell them apart. But God cannot be confused by a crowd. So the reason for the separation needs explaining.

phrases.english: But is there a jumble
before the Holy One, Blessed be He?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִיכָּא עִרְבּוּבְיָא קַמֵּי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason for the separation described in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for each nation to enter separately.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Nothing can be confused or mixed up before God, so separating the nations seems pointless.

steps.title: The separation is for the nations, so they can hear
steps.stepSummary: The separation is not for God's sake. It is so the nations won't be mixed together and each can hear what God says to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is so that they will not be mixed up with each other, so that they will hear what He says to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the separation helps the nations, not God. Each nation needs to clearly hear what is said to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed the separation was so God could tell them apart. The answer moves the purpose to the nations' side: in a mixed crowd they could not each follow what is said to them.

phrases.english: Rather, so that they will not be mixed up,
they, with each other,
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: so that they will hear what He says to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes who the separation is for: the nations, not God.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The separation seemed to be so God could tell the nations apart, which makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: The separation lets each nation hear clearly what God says to it.
steps.whatToRemember: Each nation enters separately with its scholars. This is not because God could be confused, but so each nation hears what is said to it.

steps.title: רומי enters first
steps.stepSummary: The story continues: the Roman kingdom is the first to come before God.
steps.simpleTranslation: Immediately the kingdom of Rome enters before Him first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the story and says רומי enters first. This sets up the next question: why רומי?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds a new detail to the story, the order of entry. The next steps explain why Rome goes first and where that idea comes from.

phrases.english: Immediately, there enters before Him
the kingdom of Rome, first.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיָּד נִכְנְסָה לְפָנָיו מַלְכוּת רוֹמִי תְּחִלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the side question to the story itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rome is the first nation to enter for judgment.

steps.title: Why does רומי go first?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason רומי enters first.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question: why is Rome first in line? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing has been said yet to explain the order. The גמרא wants a reason before it moves on with the story.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why Rome enters before all other nations.

steps.title: Because רומי is the most important
steps.stepSummary: רומי enters first because it is the most important nation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is important.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that Rome goes first because it is the most important nation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer rests on two ideas that still need proof: that Rome is the most important, and that the most important goes first. The next steps prove each one.

phrases.english: Because it is important.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Rome is the most important nation, so it enters first.

steps.title: How do we know רומי is the most important?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source that Rome is the most important nation.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that it is important?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for proof of the first idea in the answer: that Rome is the most important. This sets up a פסוק in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying Rome is important is a claim. The גמרא wants it grounded in a פסוק.

phrases.english: And from where do we know that it is important?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a source for the claim in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A scriptural source that Rome is the most important nation.

steps.title: The kingdom that devours the whole earth is רומי
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק in דניאל speaks of a kingdom that devours the whole earth, and רבי יוחנן says this is Rome, whose reputation spread through the whole world.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And it shall devour the whole earth, and tread it down, and break it in pieces.' רבי יוחנן said: This is wicked Rome, whose fame has spread through the whole world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק about a world-conquering kingdom, and רבי יוחנן identifies it as Rome.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק alone does not name Rome. רבי יוחנן supplies the identification, so the פסוק's picture of a kingdom that rules the whole earth becomes proof of Rome's importance.

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And it shall devour the whole earth,'
phrases.notes: דניאל 7:23

phrases.english: 'and tread it down, and break it in pieces.'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: זוֹ רוֹמִי חַיֶּיבֶת
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said: This is wicked Rome,
whose name has gone out through the whole world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דניאל describes a kingdom ruling the whole earth, and רבי יוחנן says this is Rome.

steps.title: How do we know the important one goes first?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source that the more important party enters first.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that whoever is important enters first?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא asks for proof of the second idea: that the most important one is judged first. This sets up רב חסדא's teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if Rome is the most important, that does not yet show importance decides the order. That rule needs its own source.

phrases.english: And from where do we know that whoever is important
enters first?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְנָא לַן דְּמַאן דַּחֲשִׁיב עָיֵיל בְּרֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a source for the second idea behind step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that the more important party is judged first.

steps.title: רב חסדא: the king is judged before the community
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא teaches that when a king and a community are judged, the king goes first. He learns it from a פסוק that mentions 'His servant' before 'His people ישראל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב חסדא said: a king and a community — the king enters for judgment first, as it says: 'To do the judgment of His servant and the judgment of His people Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with רב חסדא's rule that a king is judged before the people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, the judgment of the king ('His servant') is mentioned before the judgment of the people. רב חסדא reads this order as the order of judgment, showing that the more important one goes first.

keyTerms.meaning: In line with what רב חסדא said

phrases.english: In line with Rav Chisda, for Rav Chisda said:
A king and a community —
the king enters first for judgment,
as it is said: 'To do the judgment of His servant'
phrases.notes: מלכים א 8:59. 'His servant' is the king, and he is mentioned first.

phrases.english: 'and the judgment of His people Israel, etc.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב חסדא's rule that the king is judged before the community, learned from the order of the פסוק.

steps.title: Why should the king be judged first?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב חסדא's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why it makes sense for the king to go first. This sets up two possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We now have a source for the rule, but not the logic. The גמרא wants to understand why the king should come first.

phrases.english: And what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the logic behind step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the king is judged before the community.

steps.title: Two reasons the king goes first
steps.stepSummary: Either it is not respectful for a king to wait outside, or the king is judged before God's anger grows from the sins of the community.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: it is not proper for the king to sit outside. And if you want, say: so he is judged before the anger grows strong.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two possible reasons for the king going first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason is about honor: a king should not be left waiting outside. The second is about protecting the king: if the people were judged first, God's anger at their sins might grow, and the king would face a harsher judgment.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (introduces one possible answer)

phrases.english: If you want, say:
it is not proper conduct to sit
for the king, outside,
and if you want, say:
before the fierce anger grows.
phrases.notes: He means God's anger, which could grow while hearing the sins of the people.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: לָאו אוֹרַח אַרְעָא לְמֵיתַב מַלְכָּא מֵאַבָּרַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11 with two options.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Either for the king's honor, or so that he is judged before God's anger grows.
steps.whatToRemember: Rome goes first because it is the most important nation (from דניאל and רבי יוחנן), and the important one goes first (from רב חסדא's king-and-community rule).

steps.title: God asks רומי what it did
steps.stepSummary: Back in the story, the הקדוש ברוך הוא asks רומי what it spent its time doing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to them: With what did you busy yourselves?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the story. God questions Rome, and this sets up Rome's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The side questions about order are finished. Now the actual judgment starts, and Rome must show what it did to earn reward.

keyTerms.meaning: You busied yourselves, you were occupied

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to them:
With what did you busy yourselves?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: בְּמַאי עֲסַקְתֶּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the story after the side discussion of steps 5-12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God asks Rome what it occupied itself with.

steps.title: רומי claims it built everything for ישראל's sake
steps.stepSummary: רומי answers that it built many markets and bathhouses and gathered much silver and gold, all so ישראל could be free to learn תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say before Him: Master of the World, we set up many markets, we made many bathhouses, we gathered much silver and gold, and we did all of it only for ישראל, so they could busy themselves with תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: Rome answers God's question and tries to claim a share in the reward for תורה learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story promised reward to whoever engaged in תורה. Rome cannot say it learned, so it claims it built a comfortable world for ישראל so they could learn. This sets up whether God will accept the claim.

keyTerms.meaning: That they would busy themselves with תורה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as the גמרא agreeing with Rome. This is only Rome's claim, and God has not yet answered it.

phrases.english: They say before Him: Master of the World,
we set up many marketplaces,
we made many bathhouses,
we gathered much silver and gold,
and we did all of them only
for the sake of Israel,
so that they would busy themselves with Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rome's reply to God's question in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rome claims its markets, bathhouses and wealth were all built so ישראל could learn תורה.

steps.title: God rejects רומי's claim of doing it all for ישראל
steps.stepSummary: הקדוש ברוך הוא calls רומי fools. He says their markets and bathhouses were built for themselves, and the silver and gold belong to Him anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Holy One, Blessed be He, says to them: Fools of the world! Everything you did, you did for yourselves. You set up markets to put prostitutes in them, and bathhouses to pamper yourselves. And the silver and gold are Mine, as the פסוק says: 'Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says ה׳ צבאות.'
steps.whatsHappening: הקדוש ברוך הוא answers רומי's claim from step 14 and knocks down every part of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רומי said its markets, bathhouses and wealth were all for ישראל's benefit. God answers each item: the markets were for sin, the bathhouses were for their own pleasure, and the gold was never theirs to give. Their claim of doing a favor for ישראל collapses.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to them:
Fools of the world!

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל מַה שֶּׁעֲשִׂיתֶם לְצוֹרֶךְ עַצְמְכֶם עֲשִׂיתֶם,
phrases.english: Everything you did, you did for your own needs.
You set up markets to place prostitutes in them,
bathhouses to pamper yourselves in them,
and silver and gold are Mine,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״לִי הַכֶּסֶף וְלִי הַזָּהָב נְאֻם ה׳ צְבָאוֹת״.
phrases.english: as it says: 'Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says the Lord of hosts.'
phrases.notes: חגי 2:8

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: שׁוֹטִים שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly refutes רומי's claim from step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects every part of רומי's claim (markets, bathhouses, silver and gold).
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Their deeds were selfish, and the wealth was God's to begin with, so it was no favor to ישראל.

steps.title: None of you can claim to have studied תורה
steps.stepSummary: God continues: no one in רומי can 'declare this,' and 'this' means תורה, as shown from a פסוק about the תורה משה set before ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there anyone among you who can declare 'this'? As the פסוק says: 'Who among them can declare this?' And 'this' means only תורה, as it says: 'And this is the Torah that משה set.'
steps.whatsHappening: God adds the main point: the nations have nothing to show in תורה, and the גמרא proves from פסוקים that 'this' means תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ישעיה asks 'who among them can declare this?' The גמרא links the word 'זאת' to the פסוק 'וזאת התורה,' so the question really means: who among you has תורה? That is the only thing that counts, and רומי has none.

keyTerms.meaning: Is there anything / is there anyone (a question word)

steps.confusionAlert: The word 'זאת' (this) seems vague on its own. The גמרא gives it meaning by finding the same word in another פסוק, where it clearly refers to the תורה.

phrases.english: Is there anyone among you who can declare 'this'?
As it says: 'Who among them can declare this?'
phrases.notes: ישעיה 43:9

phrases.english: And 'this' means nothing other than תורה,
as it says: 'And this is the Torah that Moses set.'
phrases.notes: דברים 4:44

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues God's rejection and grounds it in פסוקים.
steps.raayaObject: That the nations have no share in תורה, the only thing that brings reward.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיה 43:9 ('מי בכם יגיד זאת') together with דברים 4:44 ('וזאת התורה').

steps.title: רומי leaves disappointed
steps.stepSummary: Right away, רומי leaves in disappointment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Immediately they left disappointed.
steps.whatsHappening: This closes the רומי part of the story: their claim failed, and they walk out let down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After God's answer, רומי has nothing left to say. Their leaving shows that a claim built on selfish deeds earns no reward.
steps.whatToRemember: רומי claimed its building and wealth were for ישראל's תורה, but God showed it was all for itself, and it had no תורה of its own. So רומי left empty-handed.

phrases.english: Immediately they left disappointed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the רומי section after God's rebuttal.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רומי's claim is rejected, and it leaves with no reward.

steps.title: פרס enters after רומי
steps.stepSummary: רומי leaves, and the kingdom of פרס comes in next.
steps.simpleTranslation: The kingdom of Rome left, and the kingdom of Persia entered after it.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves to the next nation: פרס now comes before God. This also sets up the גמרא's question about why פרס is second.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The order of the nations is not random. By saying פרס comes right after רומי, the story sets up the question of what makes פרס next in line.

phrases.english: The kingdom of Rome left,
and the kingdom of Persia entered after it.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָצָאת מַלְכוּת רוֹמִי, וְנִכְנְסָה מַלְכוּת פָּרַס אַחֲרֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רומי's exit to the next nation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פרס is the second nation to be judged, after רומי.

steps.title: Why does פרס come second?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why פרס is the one to enter after רומי.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses the story to ask why פרס specifically goes next. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא explained why the most important kingdom goes first. Now it wants to know what puts פרס in second place.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the order stated in step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why פרס is the second nation to enter.

steps.title: פרס is the next most important
steps.stepSummary: פרס goes second because it is the next most important kingdom after רומי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is the most important one after it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the nations come in order of importance, and פרס is second.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same rule that put רומי first: the more important kingdom is judged earlier. פרס ranks right after רומי, so it comes next.

phrases.english: Because it is the important one after it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: פרס is the next most important kingdom after רומי.

steps.title: How do we know פרס is second?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source that פרס ranks second.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wants proof that פרס really is the second most important kingdom. The proof comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying פרס is second is not enough; the גמרא looks for a פסוק that shows it.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do we know?

phrases.english: And from where do we know this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a source for the answer in step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that פרס is the second kingdom.

steps.title: דניאל's second beast, the bear, is פרס
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק in דניאל describes a second beast like a bear, and רב יוסף teaches that this is פרס, listing four ways they are like a bear.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And behold another beast, a second, like a bear.' And רב יוסף taught: These are the Persians, who eat and drink like a bear, are fleshy like a bear, grow their hair long like a bear, and have no rest like a bear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves פרס is second from דניאל's vision, where the second beast is a bear, and רב יוסף explains that the bear means פרס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls the bear the 'second' beast, which shows second place. רב יוסף then shows the bear stands for פרס by listing four bear-like traits of the Persians. Together they prove פרס is the second kingdom.
steps.whyThisMatters: The vision of the four beasts in דניאל is a key source for ranking the great kingdoms, and the גמרא uses it to explain the order of the nations at the final judgment.

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״וַאֲרוּ חֵיוָא אָחֳרִי תִּנְיָנָא דָּמְיָא לְדֹב״,
phrases.english: As it is written: 'And behold another beast, a second, like a bear.'
phrases.notes: דניאל 7:5

phrases.english: And Rav Yosef taught: These are the Persians,
who eat and drink like a bear,
and are heavy with flesh like a bear,
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and grow their hair long like a bear,
and have no rest, like a bear.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: ״וַאֲרוּ חֵיוָא אָחֳרִי תִּנְיָנָא דָּמְיָא לְדֹב״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source requested in step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That פרס is the second most important kingdom.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דניאל 7:5 (the second beast, like a bear), explained by רב יוסף as referring to the Persians.

steps.title: God asks Persia what it did
steps.stepSummary: הקדוש ברוך הוא asks פרס what it spent its time doing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Holy One, Blessed be He, says to them: With what did you occupy yourselves?
steps.whatsHappening: Back in the story, God asks פרס the same question He asked רומי. This sets up פרס's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The judgment of פרס follows the same pattern as רומי's. Each nation is asked what it did, and will be measured by its answer.

keyTerms.meaning: With what did you occupy yourselves?

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, says to them:
With what did you occupy yourselves?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֹמֵר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: בְּמַאי עֲסַקְתֶּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the story after the side discussion of steps 19-22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פרס is asked to account for its deeds, just like רומי.

steps.title: פרס claims its bridges, cities and wars were for ישראל
steps.stepSummary: פרס answers that it built many bridges, conquered many cities and fought many wars, all so ישראל could learn תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say before Him: Master of the Universe, we built many bridges, we conquered many cities, we fought many wars, and we did all of it only for ישראל, so that they would be busy with תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: פרס gives its answer, claiming, like רומי did, that all its achievements were for ישראל's sake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פרס lists different deeds than רומי (bridges, conquests, wars), but makes the same claim: it all helped ישראל learn תורה. The reader already expects God to test this claim the way He tested רומי's.

keyTerms.meaning: So that they would be busy with תורה

phrases.english: They say before Him: Master of the Universe,
we built many bridges,
we conquered many cities,
we fought many wars,

phrases.aramaic: וְכוּלָּם לֹא עָשִׂינוּ אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: and we did all of them only for the sake of Israel,
so that they would be busy with Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹמְרִים לְפָנָיו: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, הַרְבֵּה גְּשָׁרִים גָּשַׁרְנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: פרס answers God's question from step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פרס claims its bridges, conquests and wars were all for ישראל's תורה learning.

steps.title: ה׳ shows that פרס acted only for itself
steps.stepSummary: הקדוש ברוך הוא answers פרס: the bridges were for tolls, the cities were for forced labor, and the wars were really won by Him.
steps.simpleTranslation: ה׳ says to them: Everything you did, you did for yourselves. You built bridges to collect tolls. You took cities to force their people to work for you. And the wars? I fought them, as the פסוק says, 'ה׳ is a man of war.'
steps.whatsHappening: ה׳ takes apart each of the three claims פרס just made in step 24, one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פרס claimed that bridges, cities and wars were all for ישראל's sake. ה׳ shows that the bridges and cities served פרס's own profit. The wars do not count for פרס at all, because ה׳ is the One who really won them.

keyTerms.meaning: forced labor demanded by the government
a man of war, a warrior

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, says to them:
Everything that you did,
you did for your own needs.
You set up bridges
to collect tolls from them;
cities, to use their people for forced labor;
and the wars, I fought them,
as it says: "ה׳ is a man of war."
phrases.notes: שמות 15:3

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: כׇּל מַה שֶּׁעֲשִׂיתֶם לְצוֹרֶךְ עַצְמְכֶם עֲשִׂיתֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: ה׳ rejects פרס's claim from step 24, point by point.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פרס's works were selfish, and the victories in its wars belong to ה׳.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects every part of פרס's claim (bridges, cities, wars).
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The bridges and cities served פרס's own profit, and the wars were won by ה׳, so none of it was done for ישראל.

steps.title: פרס has no תורה to show, so they leave disappointed
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ asks whether any of them can point to תורה they learned, proves from פסוקים that 'זאת' means תורה, and פרס leaves in shame.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there anyone among you who can declare 'this'? As the פסוק says, 'Who among you can declare this.' And 'this' means only תורה, as it says, 'And this is the תורה that משה set.' Right away they leave from before Him disappointed.
steps.whatsHappening: ה׳ gives the real test: did you learn תורה yourselves? פרס has nothing to answer, so they leave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'זאת' in ישעיהו is explained by the same word in דברים, where it plainly refers to תורה. So the only thing that counts is personal תורה learning, and פרס has none. This closes the scene with פרס, just as the scene with רומי ended.

keyTerms.meaning: 'this'; here it is read as meaning תורה

phrases.english: Is there anyone among you who can declare "this"?
As it says: "Who among you can declare this."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 43:9

phrases.english: And "this" means nothing other than תורה,
as it says: "And this is the תורה that משה set."
phrases.notes: דברים 4:44

phrases.english: Immediately they leave from before Him disappointed.
phrases.notes: Literally "with a deflated soul": they walk out crushed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting פרס's deeds, ה׳ points to what is missing, תורה, and the scene with פרס ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only real תורה learning counts, and פרס has none.

steps.title: Why does פרס try after seeing רומי fail?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why פרס bothers to come forward once it saw that רומי's claims got nowhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: But once פרס saw that everything רומי said did not help at all, why did it come in?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps back from the story and asks a logic question about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רומי made a similar claim and was turned away. It seems pointless for פרס to try the same thing. The גמרא wants to know what made פרס think it would do better.

phrases.english: But since it saw,
the kingdom of פרס, about the kingdom of רומי,
that its claims did not help at all,
what is the reason it comes in?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דַּחֲזָית מַלְכוּת פָּרַס לְמַלְכוּת רוֹמִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the logic of the story told in steps 23-26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What made פרס think its claim would succeed after רומי's failed?

steps.title: פרס thinks it has a better claim than רומי
steps.stepSummary: פרס reasons that רומי destroyed the בית המקדש, while פרס built it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: They destroyed the בית המקדש, and we built it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: פרס believed its record was different from רומי's, so it hoped to succeed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פרס is not copying רומי's failed claim. It thinks it has a stronger case, because it helped build the בית המקדש, while רומי destroyed it.

phrases.english: They say:
They destroyed the בית המקדש,
phrases.notes: "They" means רומי. This is the second בית המקדש, which was built while פרס ruled.

phrases.english: and we built it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: אִינְהוּ סָתְרִי בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ וַאֲנַן בָּנִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: פרס thought its claim was stronger, since it built the בית המקדש that רומי destroyed.

steps.title: The same happens with every nation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds that the same back-and-forth takes place with each nation in turn.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the same is true for each and every nation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא widens the story: every nation comes, makes its claim, and is turned away. This sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now only רומי and פרס were described. Now we learn that all the nations go through the same scene, which leads right into the question of why the later ones bother to try.

phrases.english: And the same is true for each and every nation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the pattern of רומי and פרס to all nations.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every nation comes forward and is rejected in the same way.

steps.title: Why do the other nations try after the first ones failed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the remaining nations come forward after seeing רומי and פרס fail.
steps.simpleTranslation: But once they saw that the earlier ones' claims did not help at all, why do they come in?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats its earlier question, now about all the other nations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פרס had a special reason, since it built the בית המקדש. The other nations have no such claim, so why would they hope to succeed after two failures?

keyTerms.meaning: the earlier ones, the first ones

phrases.english: But since they saw about the earlier ones,
phrases.notes: "The earlier ones" are רומי and פרס.

phrases.english: that their claims did not help at all,
what is the reason they come in?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דַּחֲזוֹ לְקַמָּאֵי דְּלָא מַהֲנֵי וְלָא מִידֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question as step 27, now asked about the other nations.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What makes the later nations hope to succeed?

steps.title: The other nations think they are innocent
steps.stepSummary: The other nations reason that רומי and פרס enslaved ישראל, while they did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: They think: Those nations enslaved ישראל, but we did not enslave ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the other nations believe they have a cleaner record than the first two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nations think the first two were rejected because they oppressed ישראל. Since they never did that, they hope to be judged more kindly.

phrases.english: They think: Those ones enslaved ישראל,
but we did not enslave ישראל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They think they are better off because they never enslaved ישראל.

steps.title: Why are only רומי and פרס named?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רומי and פרס are singled out by name while the other nations are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about these, who are counted as important, and what is different about those, who are not counted as important?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the story names only two kingdoms and lumps all the rest together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story gives רומי and פרס their own scenes, while everyone else gets only 'and the same for every nation.' The גמרא wants the reason for this difference in importance.

phrases.english: What is different about these, who are counted as important,
phrases.notes: "These" means רומי and פרס, who got their own scenes.

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי שְׁנָא הָנֵי דְּלָא חֲשִׁיבִי לְהוּ?
phrases.english: and what is different about those, who are not counted as important?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question about why the story treats the nations differently.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why are רומי and פרס named separately?

steps.title: רומי and פרס rule until משיח comes
steps.stepSummary: רומי and פרס are named because their rule lasts until משיח arrives.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because those ones continue in their kingship until משיח comes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that these two kingdoms are special because their power lasts all the way to the end of days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Other kingdoms rise and fall. רומי and פרס continue until משיח, so they stand out as the main powers, and the story names them on their own.

phrases.english: Because those ones continue in their kingship
until משיח comes.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּהָנָךְ מָשְׁכִי בְּמַלְכוּתַיְיהוּ עַד דְּאָתֵי מְשִׁיחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רומי and פרס rule until משיח comes, so they are the important ones.
steps.whatToRemember: פרס came forward because it built the בית המקדש. The other nations came because they never enslaved ישראל. רומי and פרס are named because their rule lasts until משיח.

steps.title: The nations claim they never received the תורה
steps.stepSummary: The nations argue to ה׳ that they were never given the תורה, so they cannot be blamed for not keeping it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say before Him: Master of the World, did You give us the תורה and we did not accept it?
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves on: the nations now make a new argument, that they were never offered the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the nations argued about their good deeds. Now they switch to a defense: it is unfair to judge us on תורה we never got. This is the claim the גמרא will challenge next.

phrases.english: They say before Him: Master of the World,
did You give it to us and we did not accept it?
phrases.notes: "It" is the תורה. They mean: You never gave it to us at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹמְרִים לְפָנָיו: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, כְּלוּם נָתַתָּ לָנוּ וְלֹא קִיבַּלְנוּהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the courtroom story after the side questions of steps 27-33.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The nations claim they were never offered the תורה.

steps.title: The פסוקים show ה׳ came to שעיר and תימן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the nations' claim using פסוקים that describe ה׳ coming from שעיר and תימן when He gave the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can they really say that? But it is written: 'And he said: ה׳ came from סיני and shone forth from שעיר to them,' and it is written: 'God comes from תימן, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the nations' claim by bringing two פסוקים about the giving of the תורה that mention other places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If ה׳ gave the תורה only at סיני, why do these פסוקים say He came from שעיר and תימן? Those places belong to other nations. This suggests the nations were offered the תורה after all.

phrases.english: But can they say this?
But is it not written: "And he said: Hashem came from סיני,
phrases.notes: דברים 33:2

phrases.english: and shone forth from שעיר to them."
And it is written: "God comes from תימן, etc."
phrases.notes: חבקוק 3:3. The "etc." goes on: "and the Holy One from mount פארן."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the nations' claim from step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: The nations' claim that they were never offered the תורה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: פסוקים about the giving of the תורה mention ה׳ coming from other nations' lands, which shows the תורה was offered there too.

steps.title: What was ה׳ doing in שעיר and פארן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why ה׳ would go to שעיר and פארן, since the תורה was given at סיני.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did He need in שעיר, and what did He need in פארן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sharpens the challenge by asking what ה׳ was doing in those places. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה was given at סיני, not in שעיר or פארן. So the mention of those places needs explaining. The expected answer is that ה׳ offered the תורה to those nations, which would disprove the nations' claim.

keyTerms.meaning: what did He need, what was He doing

phrases.english: What did He need in שעיר,
and what did He need in פארן?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בָּעֵי בְּשֵׂעִיר, וּמַאי בָּעֵי בְּפָארָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws out the meaning of the פסוקים in step 35 to build the challenge.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why do the פסוקים place ה׳ in שעיר and פארן at the giving of the תורה?
steps.confusionAlert: The תורה was not given in שעיר or פארן; it was given at סיני. That is exactly why the גמרא asks what ה׳ was doing in those places.

steps.title: ה׳ offered the תורה to every nation
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that ה׳ went to שעיר and פארן because He offered the תורה to every nation. They all refused it until ישראל accepted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: This teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, brought the תורה around to every nation and language. None of them accepted it, until He came to ישראל, and they accepted it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from the previous step: why would ה׳ go to שעיר and פארן? He went there to offer the תורה to those nations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer finishes the challenge against the nations. They said 'we were never given the תורה.' Now we see the תורה was offered to them, and they refused it. So their excuse falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: He took it around (He offered the תורה from place to place)
nation and language (every people in the world)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan says:
This teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, took it around
phrases.notes: "It" means the תורה. He brought it to each nation, which is why the פסוק mentions שעיר and פארן.

phrases.english: to every nation and language,
but they did not accept it,
until He came to Israel and they accepted it!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁהֶחְזִירָהּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 36 and completes the challenge of step 35.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why ה׳ went to שעיר and פארן if the תורה was given at סיני.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He went there to offer the תורה to those nations, and they refused it.

steps.title: The nations' claim restated: we never accepted and then broke it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes what the nations really argue. They are not saying 'we never received it.' They are saying 'we never accepted it and then failed to keep it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what they say: Did we ever accept the תורה and then not keep it?
steps.whatsHappening: Since the first excuse failed, the גמרא gives a new version of the nations' argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nations now admit they were offered the תורה. Their point is that you can only be blamed for breaking a promise you actually made, and they never made one.

keyTerms.meaning: did we at all? (introduces a question that expects 'no')

phrases.english: Rather, this is what they say:
Did we accept it and then not fulfill it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Re-explains the nations' claim after step 37 knocked down the first version.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The nations were claiming the תורה was never offered to them.
steps.terutzMaskana: The nations are claiming they never committed to the תורה, so they cannot be blamed for breaking it.

steps.title: Their own words defeat them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the new excuse. Refusing to accept the תורה is itself the problem: why didn't you accept it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But this very claim is their downfall: why didn't you accept it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the nations' new excuse actually works against them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'we never accepted it' only admits that they turned the תורה down. The refusal itself is something they can be blamed for.

phrases.english: But on this itself is their downfall:
Why didn't you accept it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the restated claim of step 38.
steps.kashyaTarget: The nations' claim that they never accepted the תורה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Refusing to accept is itself a failing, so the claim admits guilt instead of excusing it.

steps.title: The nations' final claim: you never forced us
steps.stepSummary: The nations argue that ישראל only accepted the תורה because ה׳ forced them with a mountain. If ה׳ had forced the nations the same way, they would have accepted it too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what they say before Him: Master of the World, did You hold a mountain over us like a barrel, and we still did not accept it, the way You did for ישראל?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third and final version of the nations' argument. They claim they were not treated the same as ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nations say it is unfair to compare them to ישראל. ישראל were pressured into accepting, and the nations were not. Their refusal was only because they were given a free choice.

keyTerms.meaning: You turned upside down / held over

phrases.english: Rather, this is what they say before Him:
Master of the World,
did You hold a mountain over us like a barrel
and we still did not accept it,
as You did for Israel?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the claim that step 39 rejected with a stronger one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The nations simply admitted they never accepted the תורה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The nations argue they were not forced the way ישראל were, so their refusal is not comparable.

steps.title: Source for the mountain held over Israel
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the פסוק and רב דימי בר חמא's teaching. ה׳ held הר סיני over ישראל and threatened them if they would not accept the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And they stood at the bottom of the mountain.' And רב דימי בר חמא said: This teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, held the mountain over ישראל like a barrel. He said to them: If you accept the תורה, good. If not, there will be your burial!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains where the nations got the idea that ישראל were forced. It brings the source for the mountain held over them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says ישראל stood 'בתחתית ההר', literally underneath the mountain. רב דימי בר חמא reads this to mean the mountain was lifted over them. This gives the nations' claim a real basis.

keyTerms.meaning: at the bottom of (underneath) the mountain

steps.confusionAlert: ה׳'s answer in the next step does not deny that the mountain was held over ישראל. He rejects the nations' argument that they would have kept the תורה if they had been forced.

phrases.english: As it is written: "And they stood at the bottom of the mountain,"
phrases.notes: שמות 19:17. Literally "underneath the mountain," which is the key to the teaching that follows.

phrases.english: and Rav Dimi bar Chama said:
This teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, held
the mountain over Israel like a barrel,
and He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: אִם אַתֶּם מְקַבְּלִין אֶת הַתּוֹרָה — מוּטָב,
phrases.english: If you accept the Torah, good;
and if not, there will be your burial!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind the nations' claim in step 40.
steps.raayaObject: That ישראל were pressured to accept the תורה by a mountain held over them.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 19:17 as explained by רב דימי בר חמא.

steps.title: ה׳ answers: you didn't even keep the seven מצוות
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ rejects the nations' excuse. They did accept the שבע מצוות בני נח, and they did not keep even those.
steps.simpleTranslation: Immediately the Holy One, Blessed be He, says to them: The first things will tell us, as it says: 'And let them announce to us the first things.' The seven מצוות that you did accept, where did you keep them?
steps.whatsHappening: ה׳ answers the nations' final claim and shows it does not help them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nations said they would have kept the תורה if they had been made to accept it. ה׳ points to the seven מצוות they did accept long before. They did not keep those either, so their claim is not believable. The proof comes from the same פסוק in ישעיהו that the sugya has been reading.

keyTerms.meaning: the first things (here: the earlier מצוות)
they will let us hear / tell us
the seven מצוות of בני נח

steps.whatToRemember: The nations try three excuses: we never got the תורה, we never accepted it, and You never forced us. Each one fails. In the end ה׳ points out that they did not even keep the seven מצוות they had accepted.

phrases.aramaic: מִיָּד אוֹמֵר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: Immediately the Holy One, Blessed be He, says to them:
The first things will let us hear,
as it says: "And let them announce to us the first things,"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 43:9

phrases.english: the seven מצוות that you accepted,
phrases.notes: These are the שבע מצוות בני נח, the "first things" that came before the תורה.

phrases.english: where did you keep them?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיָּד אוֹמֵר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת יַשְׁמִיעוּנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refutes the nations' claim from steps 40-41.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The nations' claim that they would have kept the תורה if they had been forced.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: They did not keep even the seven מצוות they accepted, so their claim is not believable.

steps.title: How do we know the nations did not keep their seven מצוות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source showing that the nations did not keep the שבע מצוות בני נח.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that they did not keep them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for proof of ה׳'s claim from the last step, that the nations did not keep their seven מצוות. This question sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 42, ה׳ said the nations accepted the שבע מצוות בני נח and did not keep them. The גמרא wants a source for the second half of that claim, that they did not keep them.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? This asks for a source.
They kept them, they fulfilled them

phrases.english: And from where do we know that they did not keep them?
phrases.notes: "Them" means the שבע מצוות בני נח from the last step.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a source for ה׳'s claim in step 42 that the nations did not keep the seven מצוות.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that the nations did not keep the שבע מצוות בני נח.

steps.title: רב יוסף's reading of the פסוק‎: ה׳ saw and released them
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף reads a פסוק in חבקוק‎: ה׳ saw that the nations did not keep their seven מצוות, so He released them from those מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף taught: "He stands and measures the earth, He sees and makes the nations tremble." What did He see? He saw the seven מצוות that the children of נח accepted and did not keep. Since they did not keep them, He got up and released them from them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the question with a פסוק. He explains that ה׳ "saw" the nations failing to keep their seven מצוות, and so He released them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key word is וַיַּתֵּר. רב יוסף reads it as related to הֶתֵּר, meaning release. ה׳ looked and saw that the nations did not keep their מצוות, which proves the claim from step 42. It also adds a new idea: as a result, ה׳ released them from those מצוות.

keyTerms.meaning: A word in the פסוק that רב יוסף reads as "and He released"
He released them, He freed them from the obligation
The seven מצוות given to all humanity, the children of נח

steps.confusionAlert: "He released them" sounds like a reward for the nations, and that is exactly what bothers the גמרא. The next step challenges this. מר בריה דרבינא begins his answer at the very end of this amud, and it continues on the next amud.

phrases.english: As רב יוסף teaches:
"He stands and measures the earth,
phrases.notes: חבקוק 3:6

phrases.english: He sees and makes the nations tremble."
phrases.notes: רב יוסף hears וַיַּתֵּר as "He released," like the word הֶתֵּר. That reading is the whole proof.

phrases.english: What did He see?
He saw the seven מצוות
that the children of נח accepted upon themselves
and they did not keep them.
Since they did not keep them,
He got up and released them from them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 43 with a פסוק explained by רב יוסף.
steps.raayaObject: Proves that the nations did not keep the שבע מצוות בני נח.
steps.raayaSupportSource: חבקוק 3:6, read by רב יוסף‎: ה׳ "saw" they did not keep the מצוות and "released" (וַיַּתֵּר) them.

steps.title: Does a sinner gain from his sin?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף: if the nations were released because they broke the מצוות, then they gained from sinning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did they gain from this? If so, we find that a sinner is rewarded!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב יוסף's idea that the nations were released from their מצוות. That would mean breaking the rules got them a reward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being freed from obligations sounds like a benefit. If the nations earned that benefit by failing to keep the מצוות, then sinning paid off. That cannot be right, so the גמרא needs to explain what "He released them" really means.

keyTerms.meaning: Did they really gain? Did they come out ahead?
We find. This means: we would end up with a strange result.
A sinner who is rewarded, someone who profits from doing wrong

phrases.english: Did they really gain from this?
If so, we find that a sinner profits!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the result of רב יוסף's reading in step 44.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's statement that ה׳ released the nations from the seven מצוות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A release from obligations is a gain. If they got it by not keeping the מצוות, then a sinner profits from sinning, and that is unacceptable.

steps.title: מר בריה דרבינא steps in to answer
steps.stepSummary: מר בריה דרבינא is introduced to answer the question of whether a sinner gains.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר, the son of רבינא, said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line only introduces the answer. The words of מר בריה דרבינא's answer continue on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא brings an אמורא to resolve the problem from step 45. He will explain what "He released them" means in a way that does not reward the sinners.
